paper.citation: Fiorini S, Guglielmetti M, Neri LCL, Correale L, Tagliabue A, Ferraris C. Mediterranean Diet and athletic performance in elite and competitive athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Nutrition, Metabolism and Cardiovascular Diseases. 2025.
paper.abstract: Systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42023459039, PRISMA) of 9 studies with 192 mostly male competitive or elite adult athletes from several sports, searched to October 2024. Five studies reported an effect of the Mediterranean Diet on performance (four positive), and the random-effects meta-analysis of performance outcomes showed no effect (SMD 0.00, 95% CI -0.26 to 0.25).
paper.tldr: Across 9 small, mostly observational studies in athletes, Mediterranean Diet adherence was loosely associated with some performance measures, but the pooled meta-analysis found no effect on performance.
paper.methods: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 9 studies from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library, with risk of bias assessed by RoB 2.0, Robins-I and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The included designs were five cross-sectional studies, two randomised trials, one longitudinal experimental study and one longitudinal study, with sample sizes of 10 to 43 athletes, and performance outcomes were pooled as standardised mean differences.
paper.findings: Narratively, MedDiet adherence was positively related to anaerobic/aerobic power and explosive strength, and five studies reported an impact on performance, four of them positive. The pooled performance analysis showed no MedDiet effect (SMD 0.00, 95% CI -0.26 to 0.25), with substantial heterogeneity for countermovement jump results, and body composition could be pooled from only one study.
paper.limitations: Only 9 studies with 192 participants were included, using varied designs, sports, performance tests and adherence tools. Most studies had high risk of bias, mainly in outcome measurement, dietary data were largely self-reported, all studies were from Spain or Italy, and supplement use was often unreported or uncontrolled.
paper.practicalImplications: This review does not justify promising performance gains from a Mediterranean-style diet. It supports the pattern as a sound dietary approach for athletes, while the performance evidence remains inconclusive and supplement use cannot be separated from diet effects.
paper.athleteDev: A Mediterranean-style eating pattern can be a reasonable dietary framework to discuss with athletes, but this review shows no pooled performance benefit. Any performance change seen with the diet should be interpreted cautiously given the small, varied and mostly observational evidence.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot be used for return-to-sport decisions.
